name: Hay's Brown
lede: Hay's Brown is a muted, warm brown that Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary names for a person, one of six Hay's colors in his book, and the only one the Inter-Society Color Council never repeated.

sections.title: One of six colors named Hay's
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Hay's Brown at hex #755B4E among the names he credits to a person [1]. It shares its possessive with five other colors in the same book: [[hay-s-green|Hay's Green]], [[hay-s-lilac|Hay's Lilac]], [[hay-s-maroon|Hay's Maroon]] and [[hay-s-russet|Hay's Russet]], but Ridgway never names the Hay he means, so the connection is undocumented in our sources [1]. Unlike those five, the 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog does not repeat Hay's Brown; by our own nearest match to its 1955 color blocks it would fall closest to grayish brown, 4.8 units off, but that block itself carries a different name [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[pale-brown|Pale Brown]], only 3.1 units away and yellower [1]. [[sandalwood|Sandalwood]] and [[nutmeg|Nutmeg]] sit a little further out [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[umber|Umber]], 5.3 units off [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this brown in 4.38% of 23,781 paintings, 1,042 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 647 [2]. That makes it more common than 86% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 5.6% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.6 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits hidden, in 48% of its 647 appearances, by lightness rank rather than by brand [2]. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec is its most devoted painter here, holding it in 6 of 36 works, 4.5 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from; John Singer Sargent carries it in 19 of his 287 [2]. Our earliest match dates to the year 960, 952 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
